# Methods

Let $N_{it}$ be the number of claims in tract $i$ and year $t$, $e_{it}$ the exposure in policy-years, and $\mathbf{x}_{it}$ the vector of features built from policy information known at inception. All three models predict the expected count $\mu_{it}$ with $\log e_{it}$ as an offset, so they share the same target and the same exposure adjustment.

The three models use the same feature set, so that differences in performance come from the model and not from the information it receives. The GLMs receive transformed versions of the features where needed (for example the logarithm of mean coverage, and an indicator for missing values), while LightGBM uses them directly, since trees are insensitive to monotone transformations.

## Poisson GLM

$$
N_{it}\sim\text{Poisson}(\mu_{it}),\qquad \log\mu_{it}=\log e_{it}+\mathbf{x}_{it}^\top\boldsymbol\beta
$$ {#eq-poisson}

The Poisson GLM is the reference model for claim counts. The log link makes the effects multiplicative, and the offset turns the model into a model of the claim rate per policy-year, so tracts with different exposure are directly comparable. It assumes that the variance equals the mean, which the next model relaxes.

## Negative Binomial GLM

$$
\text{Var}(N_{it})=\mu_{it}+\alpha\mu_{it}^2
$$ {#eq-nb}

The negative binomial GLM keeps the mean structure of @eq-poisson and adds a dispersion parameter $\alpha$, estimated jointly with $\boldsymbol\beta$ by maximum likelihood. The EDA shows that claims cluster in a few event years (@fig-freq-year), so tract-year counts are likely to vary much more than a Poisson model allows. The Poisson model is the limit $\alpha \to 0$, so the comparison shows whether modelling overdispersion changes the predictions or only their uncertainty.

## LightGBM with Poisson Objective

LightGBM fits gradient boosted trees by minimizing the Poisson negative log-likelihood, with $\log e_{it}$ as initial score. The initial score plays the role of the offset, so the trees learn the log claim rate relative to exposure, as in the GLMs. Unlike the GLMs, the trees can capture non-linear effects and interactions without specifying them in advance, which is the flexibility that RQ1 evaluates.

The hyperparameters tuned are the number of leaves, the learning rate, the minimum number of observations per leaf and the share of features used per tree. The number of boosting rounds is chosen by early stopping on the validation year of each fold. All random operations use a fixed seed (42), so that results are reproducible.

## Validation

Hyperparameters and model choices are selected by forward-chaining validation inside 2010 to 2019: each fold trains on all earlier years and validates on the following year. We plan four folds: train 2010 to 2015 and validate on 2016, then validate on 2017, 2018 and 2019 in turn, each time adding the previous validation year to the training set. The validation years include both high-frequency years (2016 to 2018) and a quiet year (2019), so the selected settings are not tuned to a single regime. This respects the time order and mimics the real task of predicting future years without using future information. The final models are refitted on 2010 to 2019 with the selected settings, and the test years 2020 to 2024 are used only once, for the final evaluation.

## Metrics

All metrics are fixed in advance, before looking at the test years.

- **Poisson deviance** on the test years:
  $$
  D=2\sum_{i,t}\left[y_{it}\log\frac{y_{it}}{\hat\mu_{it}}-(y_{it}-\hat\mu_{it})\right],
  $$ {#eq-deviance}
  with $y_{it}\log(y_{it}/\hat\mu_{it})=0$ when $y_{it}=0$. It is the natural loss for count predictions and the quantity the Poisson models optimize, so it compares the three models on a common scale. Lower is better.
- **Calibration by prediction decile.** Test tract-years are grouped into ten classes of predicted frequency, and predicted and observed claims are compared in each class. This shows whether a model is biased for low-risk or high-risk tracts, which the deviance alone does not reveal.
- **Gini index.** Tract-years are sorted by predicted frequency, and the cumulative share of exposure is plotted against the cumulative share of observed claims (ordered Lorenz curve). The Gini index is twice the area between this curve and the diagonal, normalized by the value obtained when sorting by observed frequency, so that a perfect ranking scores 1. Weighting by exposure gives tracts with more policies more importance, as in a portfolio. It measures how well a model ranks tract-years from low to high risk, independently of the level of the predictions, which is what matters for risk segmentation.
- **Predicted versus observed totals per test year.** This checks aggregate bias year by year, which matters because the test window contains Hurricane Ian (2022) and Hurricane Helene (2024).

Results are reported overall and for Florida versus the other seven states, because Florida accounts for about 71% of policy records and 57% of claims and could dominate the overall metrics.

**Sensitivity check.** The models are refitted with a target that counts all claims, not only claims with a positive paid amount, to check whether the comparison depends on the claim definition.

# Findings and Discussion

No model has been fitted at this stage: the tract-year table, which all three models need, is still being built. The preliminary findings therefore come from the data and shape what we expect from the models.

The crude frequency computed in the EDA is `{python} f"{freq_train:.2f}"` paid claims per 1,000 policy-years over the training years and `{python} f"{freq_test:.2f}"` over the test years (@tbl-freq-year). A model that is well calibrated on 2010 to 2019 will thus predict too few claims in total for 2020 to 2024, whatever its type, because no feature describes the hazard of a given year. The comparison between LightGBM and the GLMs will therefore rely mostly on deviance, ranking (Gini) and calibration by decile, which measure how well each model separates risky from less risky tracts. The totals per test year will show how large the common bias is in the hurricane years.

The state-level frequencies (@tbl-freq-state) show that Florida's frequency is far below that of the other states in the training years (`{python} f"{fl_freq_train:.2f}"` against `{python} f"{other_freq_train:.2f}"` per 1,000 policy-years) but above it in the test years (`{python} f"{fl_freq_test:.2f}"` against `{python} f"{other_freq_test:.2f}"`). All models are therefore likely to under-predict Florida tracts in 2020 to 2024, and Florida holds most of the test claims. A more flexible model could learn this pattern of the training years more closely and suffer more from the reversal, or rank tracts better within each group. The split by state (RQ2) is designed to tell these cases apart.

These expectations will be tested once the models are fitted, and the results will be reported with the metrics above.
